source.title: Better and Worse with Scale: How Contextual Entrainment Diverges with Model Size
source.authors: Dikshant Kukreja; Kshitij Sah; Gautam Gupta; Avinash Anand; R. Shah; Zheng-Kui Wang; Aik Beng Ng; Erik Cambria

record.file_problem: The text includes some garbled figure text, but the paper and its tables are readable.
record.tranche_reason: Applies power-law scaling analysis to contextual entrainment, a different behavioral measure from the loss and allocation claims, and reports results in two model families.
record.gate_note: The paper reports scaling of context-induced token-logit changes, not held-out pretraining cross-entropy loss, compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, or downstream task performance. These findings are recorded under fits_no_version; they do not test any listed version.
record.test_reason: The study borrows the power-law form E(N)=a·N^b as an analysis tool and fits it to context-induced logit shifts (contextual entrainment) in Cerebras-GPT and Pythia. It reports no held-out pretraining loss, no extrapolation test, no compute allocation, no shape comparison, no other modality, and no downstream task accuracy. Entrainment is a related but different construct, so its results go under fits_no_version. T3 is not appropriate because no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that entrainment follows power laws whose sign depends on context type: larger models resist semantic and counterfactual distractors more but copy arbitrary tokens more. They say this replicates across Cerebras-GPT and Pythia, and that scaling reshapes context sensitivity rather than resolving it.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses log-log regression of parameter count against context-induced token-logit changes, rather than fitting held-out pretraining loss or optimizing parameter/token allocation against training compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted direction and exponent vary by context type; the paper also reports different exponent magnitudes between model families.

fits_no_version.finding: Distractor entrainment (∆dstr) fits power laws in model size, with negative exponents for semantic contexts (Counterfactual, Related) and positive exponents for non-semantic contexts (Random, Irrelevant). The sign split appears in both Cerebras-GPT (n=7) and Pythia (n=6), with smaller magnitudes in Pythia.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Contextual entrainment scales as a power law in parameter count, with the sign depending on whether the context is semantically meaningful.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The evidence concerns behavioral logit shifts rather than loss. The main power-law fits use only seven Cerebras-GPT and six Pythia model sizes; the paper's stated scope is decoder-only Transformers and two model families.
record.rows_left_out: The 60-row limit was reached. Omitted separately reported ∆overall (gold-minus-distractor) regression fits, gold-logit and overall-logit checkpoint measurements, no-context and with-context baseline regression blocks, and additional convergence analyses (Tables 3–6 and Figures 3, 7–8). These also concern contextual behavior rather than the listed loss/allocation versions.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss is measured against parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation of loss from small runs to larger ones.
No compute budget or parameter/token allocation.
No depth or width comparison at fixed parameter count.
No other modality or training regime; the fits are of behavioural logit shifts, not loss.
No downstream task accuracy or loss–performance relation. The no-context gold-logit scaling (b≈+0.13) is a logit, not task performance, and no row records it.
No test of fitting choices for loss exponents or the compute-optimal split.

record.verdict_notes: Thirteen Related-context rows (r01–r07 for Cerebras-GPT, r29–r34 for Pythia) carry Counterfactual no-context baselines; the corrections are in row_fixes. The delta values in those rows are correct. The power-law fits use only 6–7 points across about two orders of magnitude in N. The study touches loss-scaling claims only through borrowing the fitting form.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss scaling is measured.
No predictions of larger-run loss from smaller-run loss fits are evaluated.
No compute budget or parameter/token allocation is studied.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count is reported.
The paper studies contextual entrainment in language models, not loss scaling across modalities or training regimes.
No downstream task performance or relationship between downstream performance and pretraining loss is measured.
The paper varies context condition and model family, but does not test fitting choices or setup-dependence of loss-law exponents or compute-optimal allocation.
